in.title: Why a Gond Adivasi Community Remembers 2 Tigers as Protectors of the Household
in.description: For generations, a story about two tigers has travelled through Gond households in Madhya Pradesh’s Kanha landscape. They were called Ram and Laxman. According to the oral tradition remembered by Dayal Singh Kusre, a Gond Adivasi who worked as a cook in different parts of Kanha, the tigers once shared a household with people. People fed them, treated them with respect, and regarded them as protectors. The story survives in community memory, along with a practice of making offerings to tigers. It is not a scientific account of tiger behaviour. For Kusre, the story is inseparable from a larger understanding of nature. “Forests and wildlife are not something to be protected from a distance. Both are part of a shared landscape, where people must learn how to live alongside other species”, Kusre tells The Better India. But can cultural memory really help people negotiate their place alongside wild animals? When tigers were part of the household Kusre recalls a Gond tribal story in which Ram and Laxman occupied a place within the household’s collective memory. According to the Gond folklore, family members were instructed not to encounter the tigers when they first entered the household. A newly married bride, in particular, was told not to open a particular locked room or door. The restriction was associated with the belief that the tigers would not recognise a new family member, much as traditional households have sometimes maintained rules around interactions between younger women and senior male relatives. In the story, one daughter-in-law eventually opened the door without knowing or following the instructions. She saw the tiger’s face, and the animal left the household. Kusre recounts the tiger’s message to the family’s eldest man: he would now stay in the forest and receive his food there. The room and its closed door represent a boundary that members of the household were expected to respect. The tiger was part of the story, but so was the responsibility of people to recognise that a relationship with wildlife came with limits. The tradition also carries an idea of reciprocity. Kusre says, “The family believed that if people had food, they should ensure that the wildlife around them was fed, too” He also describes a practice of making an offering of a goat or a hen to the tiger in the forest once a year, with the belief that the animal would continue to protect the family. ‘Nature is our all’ For Kusre, reverence for Ram and Laxman is part of a wider relationship with nature. “For us, nature is our all; we bow at her feet,” he says. “If we have to cross 10 km of forests also, then we pray to nature, and the Adivasis feel confident. They trust nature for protection.” He also recalls what he describes as older Gond beliefs about encounters with tigers. “Our ancestors used to cross paths with tigers normally, but in reality, tiger spotting is difficult,” he says. Tigers are elusive, and their presence in a landscape does not necessarily mean that people regularly see them. These details belong to Kusre’s account of Gond oral tradition, but it does not suggest that people should approach, feed, or attempt to house wild tigers today. Its relevance lies in what the narrative reveals about the values through which tribal communities understand the natural world. What communities learn from living alongside wildlife Conservation biologist Shivangi Bendre, whose work focuses primarily on the Central Indian landscape, and mitigating human-wildlife conflict, says it is important to understand the everyday practices through which communities adapt to the presence of wild animals. “I think it is important to look not just at the living practices of communities, but also at their livelihoods and the different, sometimes ingenious, ways they have developed to live alongside wildlife. These practices emerge from generations of experience of sharing landscapes with wild animals,” she tells The Better India. Bendre points to communities living alongside sloth bears in Hampi as an example. Drawing insights from Wildlife Conservation Society India's report "A relational perspective of Sloth Bear - Human Relations in Hampi region of Karnataka" by Mohammed Hisham K, she says, ‘when sloth bears enter an area, people may light fires, clap or make sounds to alert the animals to their presence.” “The idea is to communicate, in a way the animals can recognise, that people are present. Rather than reacting when an encounter happens, community members use these practices to signal their presence and reduce the likelihood of a surprise encounter,” she explains. These practices or stories should not automatically be treated as universally effective or safe. Their usefulness depends on the species, local conditions, and the circumstances of an encounter. Still, Bendre says that the knowledge developed by people who live alongside wildlife deserves consideration in conservation planning. Their experiences can help researchers understand how encounters happen, what people fear and which locally developed responses may help reduce risks. When a feared animal becomes part of culture Bendre also points to Pilivesha, a traditional tiger dance practised in Karnataka, as an example of how cultural expression can shape the way people relate to wildlife. In Pilivesha, performers portray tigers through dance and elaborate body painting. The animal becomes part of a public cultural expression, represented through movement, performance and artistic skill. “What is interesting is how such cultural practices can shape the way people relate to an animal that might otherwise evoke fear,” Bendre says. In the context she describes, the tradition has helped make the tiger more familiar as a cultural symbol, with some reduction in the fear associated with its presence. Research by Rohan Sharma of WCS India, “Celebrating Nature-Culture Relationships: Documenting Cultures and Traditions of Tiger Folklore in Coastal Karnataka through the Annual Pilivesha Celebrations”, also offers context to this relationship. The research explores how the tradition does not mean that it necessarily reduces conflict with wild tigers, or that cultural familiarity can substitute for practical safety measures. It shows how an animal's place in community life can extend beyond the risks associated with encounters. Dikesh Chaudhary, project officer at The Corbett Foundation, stresses the importance of preserving such traditions as part of community history. “The idea is to save the tradition. It is a challenge, the cultural part. It is part of the history of the Gond and Baiga communities, and it is thus important,” he says. For Chaudhary, these traditions also offer a response to a question that can arise in conservation discussions: why should tigers be protected? “There are people who still may have questions: ‘Baagh kyun bachana hai?’ (Why should we save the tiger? This is the answer to that question. We should know why we need to save the tiger.” Cultural traditions cannot, on their own, explain every ecological reason for conserving a species. Tigers play a role in forest ecosystems, and their protection is connected to the wider conservation of habitats and biodiversity. But the meanings communities attach to an animal can also influence whether its continued presence is regarded as valuable. Are all traditional beliefs good for conservation? Respecting cultural memory does not mean accepting every traditional belief without question. Some beliefs may discourage the killing of animals or encourage people to regard wildlife as worthy of protection. Others may have little direct bearing on conservation. And some can create risks for people, particularly when a belief influences decisions during a medical emergency. Bendre talks about this distinction through an example she encountered in studies in Kanha, where a belief about snakebite can influence how people respond after being bitten. “The belief is that there's this one particular jari-booti(medicinal herb) that, when the person who's been bitten consumes it, the snake, wherever it is, will die and split into two halves,” she says. According to Bendre, people who believe in this remedy may turn to traditional healers rather than take the person who has been bitten to a hospital. The problem, she explains, is not that the belief exists. It is that following it may delay treatment and put the person's life at risk. “They're not really directly attacking the snake, but at the same time, that superstition may cause the person's life to be in danger,” she says. A belief that does not directly encourage people to kill a snake may have a different conservation implication from one that delays potentially life-saving medical care. The question, therefore, is not whether traditional beliefs should be accepted or rejected wholesale. It is how to recognise their significance while addressing practices that create risks. Awareness is only part of the answer “Education and awareness and primary healthcare is also something that needs to be addressed in parallel with whatever awareness that we do on the conservation front,” Bendre says. Communities need reliable information about animal behaviour, practical guidance on reducing encounters and access to appropriate support when incidents occur. Where wildlife-related risks affect livelihoods or safety, conservation efforts must also take those everyday realities seriously. The story of Ram and Laxman cannot tell us how tigers behave, whether they recognise people as family or whether feeding an animal will make it a protector. Those questions require evidence, and the story should not be treated as a guide to interacting with wild tigers. In Kusre’s telling, the tigers' departure from the household does not end the relationship. The story continues through remembrance, reverence, and the belief that the forest remains their place. Its central idea is not that wild animals should live with people, but that people must recognise their place in a landscape they share with other species. Coexistence does not mean eliminating every boundary between humans and wildlife. It means finding ways to live alongside animals while respecting their ecological needs and protecting human lives.

bd.title: Sanya and Maldives Sign Agreements to Deepen Trade and Investment Ties
bd.description: Two-day mission advances partnerships in yacht services, fisheries, and aquaculture, turning overseas outreach into commercial opportunities SANYA, China, Oct. 31, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Sanya has secured new agreements to advance trade and investment ties with the Maldives following a two-day mission focused on the blue economy, yacht services, fisheries, and aquaculture. A delegation representing the Sanya Municipal Bureau of Commerce, the Sanya Central Business District Administration, the Sanya Investment Promotion Bureau, and the Sanya Tourism Development Bureau visited the Maldives from October 27 to 28, 2026. Drawing on the favorable policies of the Hainan Free Trade Port (FTP), the delegation met with local government and business leaders to build commercial partnerships and identify projects for joint development. Sanya and Maldives Sign Agreements to Deepen Trade and Investment Ties The mission followed a visit to Sanya by a Maldivian trade delegation in August and explored how the two economies could turn their complementary industry strengths into business opportunities. On October 27, the Sanya delegation visited Alshaali Marine and Gulf Craft Maldives to discuss trade in yacht components, maintenance and refurbishment, new yacht sales, and duty-free imports — with the goal of establishing a yacht manufacturing and maintenance facility in Sanya. The delegation also met with the Maldives Ministry of Fisheries, Agriculture and Ocean Resources to strengthen links between fishing ports and develop trade routes for tuna, skipjack, and other seafood to be processed in Sanya for export to global markets. Further discussions covered aviation and tourism, tropical fruit and vegetable trade, and green energy. On October 28, the China-Maldives Investment Cooperation Forum took place in Malé. The Sanya Investment Promotion Bureau delivered a keynote presentation on blue economy partnerships, highlighting how the Hainan FTP's policy advantages and Sanya's industrial base can support new commercial links across the Indian Ocean. At the forum, the Sanya Municipal Bureau of Commerce and the Sanya Investment Promotion Bureau signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) on trade and economic cooperation with the Maldives Ministry of Economic Development, Transport and Trade. The MOU sets out a framework for long-term collaboration in trade and investment promotion, fisheries and aquaculture, the blue economy, and business matchmaking, with a focus on encouraging investment in both directions. On the same day, the Sanya Investment Promotion Bureau and the Sanya Central Business District Administration signed a Strategic Cooperation Framework Agreement with Mariculture Maldives. The partners will collaborate on breeding tropical aquaculture species, develop large-scale marine farming, and open two-way trade channels for fresh seafood. The Maldivian company plans to establish operations in Sanya, using the FTP's favorable policies to expand into the Asia-Pacific market. The delegation also held face-to-face meetings with Island Aviation Services Ltd, which operates the national airline Maldivian, and with Leo Trading to explore further business opportunities. "Our overseas outreach must deliver real results. It is not enough to reach consensus — we must turn agreements into concrete trade flows and industrial investment," said Tong Liyan, head of the Sanya delegation and Party Secretary of the Sanya Investment Promotion Bureau. She added that Sanya will provide comprehensive support for businesses entering each other's markets, helping local companies expand into Maldivian tourism and fisheries markets and inviting Maldivian businesses to see Sanya's industrial parks, ports, and business environment firsthand. The aim is to turn that interest into new investment and help Maldivian companies establish operations in the city. Drawing on its distinctive coastal assets and the international reach of the Hainan FTP, Sanya continues to expand its trade and investment ties with Indian Ocean island nations. By connecting marine industries, opening trade routes, and supporting businesses in both markets, the city aims to turn the two economies' maritime strengths into commercial success — making the ocean a bridge to new markets and mutual growth.

pg.title: How to Check Vodafone PNG Data Balance Using the Internet and Mobile Phone
pg.description: Vodafone PNG customers can check their remaining mobile internet data balance using their mobile phones or the internet. Checking your data balance regularly helps you monitor your internet usage, know how much data you have left and avoid running out of data unexpectedly. Here is a step-by-step guide explaining how to check your Vodafone PNG data balance using different methods in Papua New Guinea. METHOD 1: CHECK VODAFONE DATA BALANCE USING USSD CODE This is one of the quickest ways to check your remaining data balance. You do not need mobile internet, Wi-Fi or a smartphone to use this method. Step 1: Open the Phone or Dialler application on your mobile phone. Step 2: Enter the Vodafone balance-check code: *120# Step 3: Press the Call button using your Vodafone PNG SIM card. Step 4: Wait for the USSD menu to appear on your phone screen. Step 5: Select the option for Data Balance or Internet Balance, if displayed. Step 6: Follow the instructions to view your remaining internet data, active bundle and expiry information. METHOD 2: CHECK DATA BALANCE USING THE MY VODAFONE APP Vodafone PNG customers with smartphones can use the My Vodafone application to monitor their account balances, data subscriptions and other mobile services. Step 1: Open Google Play Store on your Android phone or Apple App Store on your iPhone. Step 2: Search for the official My Vodafone PNG application and install it. Step 3: Open the application after installation. Step 4: Enter your Vodafone PNG mobile number to register or log in. Step 5: Complete the verification process using the OTP (One-Time Password) sent to your mobile number, if requested. Step 6: After logging in, you will see your account dashboard. Step 7: Look for your available data balance and active subscriptions on the dashboard. Step 8: Select the relevant data plan or account information section to check your remaining data and bundle validity. METHOD 3: CHECK VODAFONE DATA BALANCE USING THE INTERNET You can also access Vodafone account services through an internet browser on your smartphone, tablet or computer. Step 1: Connect your device to the internet using mobile data or Wi-Fi. Step 2: Open Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox, Safari or another internet browser. Step 3: Visit the Vodafone PNG website. Step 4: Look for the My Vodafone account login option. Step 5: Enter your registered account details to sign in. Step 6: Once logged in, open your account dashboard. Step 7: Check the available account balance and data subscription information, where displayed. Step 8: Review your remaining data allowance and bundle expiry information. Note: If your data balance is not displayed on the browser dashboard, use the My Vodafone mobile application or USSD method instead. METHOD 4: CHECK VODAFONE BALANCE THROUGH SMS Vodafone customers can also request their account balance using SMS. Step 1: Open the Messages application on your mobile phone. Step 2: Create a new SMS message. Step 3: Type the following message: My Balance Step 4: Enter the recipient number: 120 Step 5: Press Send and wait for a reply containing your account balance information. METHOD 5: CHECK VODAFONE BALANCE BY CALLING You can also use Vodafone's automated telephone service to check your account balance. Step 1: Open the Phone application on your mobile phone. Step 2: Dial 120 using your Vodafone SIM card. Step 3: Press the Call button. Step 4: Follow the automated voice instructions to access your account balance information. pg.title: How to Remove a Label from All Blogger Posts – Step-by-Step Guide
pg.description: Blogger labels help organise blog posts into categories, making it easier for readers to find related content. However, there may be times when you want to remove an unwanted label from your blog, especially when reorganising your categories or cleaning up old labels. If you have many posts using the same label, removing it individually from every post can be time-consuming. This guide explains how to find posts carrying a particular label and remove it. Step 1: Log in to Your Blogger Dashboard Open Blogger. Sign in using your Google account. Select the blog you want to manage if you have multiple blogs. Step 2: Open Your Blog Posts On the left-hand menu, click Posts. You will see a list of published posts and drafts on your blog. Locate the label you want to remove from your posts. Step 3: Filter Posts by Label Click the label filter or dropdown menu above the posts list. Select the label you want to remove. Blogger will display posts associated with that particular label. This allows you to identify all posts carrying the unwanted label. Step 4: Select the Posts Click the checkbox at the top of the posts list to select the displayed posts. If Blogger displays multiple pages of posts, repeat the selection process on each page. Make sure you have identified all posts from which you want to remove the label. Step 5: Remove the Label Blogger provides bulk label-management tools, but the available options may not include a direct way to remove an existing label from multiple selected posts. If you cannot find a bulk-remove option, open each post individually: Click the post title. Locate Labels in the right-hand post settings panel. Remove the unwanted label while keeping any other labels you want to retain. Click Update to save the changes. Repeat this process for the remaining posts. Step 6: Verify That the Label Has Been Removed Return to the Blogger Posts dashboard. Open the label filter again. Select the label you removed. Check whether any posts are still associated with it. If no posts appear, the label is no longer assigned to any posts. Important Things to Remember Removing a label does not delete the blog posts. Other labels attached to the posts should remain unchanged. Removing a label from posts is different from deleting a post. If the label is still assigned to other posts, it will continue appearing in your Blogger label list. Conclusion Removing unwanted labels is a useful way to keep your Blogger website organised. Although Blogger provides bulk tools for managing posts, it does not always offer a straightforward bulk label-removal option. For blogs with hundreds or thousands of posts, an automated solution using the Blogger API may be more efficient than manually editing every post.

ae.title: One man, one journey, 28 years: Karl Bushby's walk around the world is almost complete
ae.description: LONDON: Karl Bushby is nearing the end of an epic walk around the world that he started half a lifetime ago in 1998. He was a young man of 29 at the start and now he's past middle age at 57 as he approaches his mother's home in Hull, England. He has navigated the shifting ice over the Bering Strait and swam across the Caspian Sea and English Channel, but most of the trip has been on land where he traversed dangerous jungle, rainforests, deserts, frozen tundra and battled almost every type of element imaginable. Here’s a look at Bushby's adventure, by the numbers: If fitness trackers had been around when Bushby started his trip, it's likely they couldn't have kept up with his cumulative number of steps. The total mileage Bushby put on his body is the equivalent of having run 10,000 5K road races (50,000 kilometres). Bushby initially estimated the distance could be traversed in five years. "Then you just dump a whole bucket full of reality on that,” he said. "We suspected that it was 12 years plus. And the plus was a big plus. But never in our wildest dreams would we ever have imagined 28 years.” That adds up to more than 10,220 days. When geopolitical conflicts closed off passage through Russia and Iran, Bushby decided he would swim across the Caspian Sea, the world's largest inland body of water. His 31-day crossing relied on a technique he calls "floatimming,” a hybrid of floating and swimming. He wore a flotation vest and wetsuit and plodded backward by flapping his arms in the water. Starting in Chile and ending in the U.K., he has entered or passed through 30 foreign countries before returning home. No country took longer to get through than Russia, where Bushby spent 10 years, was once detained and faced deportation for entering illegally after crossing the Bering Strait. Harsh weather only permitted a few months of travel each year and there were many bureaucratic delays. Russia denied him a visa in 2012, so Bushby spent a year walking 3,500 miles (5,600 kilometres) in protest from Los Angeles to the Russian Embassy in Washington, D.C., which eventually led to him getting the proper paperwork. Still, it ended up taking about a decade to be done with the country. The trek has taken Bushby through South America, North America, Asia and Europe - all but three of the world's seven continents. Bushby fell in love twice and had his heart broken each time. He carried on long-term romances with a woman from Colombia and another from Japan. But the relationships couldn't weather the toll of the road. Bushby estimates he went through 10 pairs of shoes traveling through the Americas but then lost track. That was 20 years ago, though, so who can blame him? "After that we were just in and out of all kinds of different stuff,” he said. The total? "A lot.”

sa.title: طالبت المليشيا بفتح الطرق فوراً.. «العفو الدولية» تحذر من تفاقم الأزمة الإنسانية في تعز
sa.description: حذرت منظمة العفو الدولية من تفاقم الأزمة الإنسانية في تعز بسبب حصار مليشيا الحوثي، مؤكدةً تعرض حياة آلاف المدنيين للخطر، في ظل تصاعد القتال واقترابه من المناطق المكتظة بالسكان. وطالبتالحوثي بفتح الطرق الرئيسية المؤدية إلى مدينة تعز والمحيطة بها فوراً. أوضاع إنسانية متدهورة وأفادت المنظمة، اليوم السبت ، بأن الحوثيين شددوا قبضتهم على مدينة تعز خلال أكتوبر، عقب قطع الطريق الرئيسي الرابط بينها وبين مدينة عدن، ما دفع الأوضاع الإنسانية نحو مزيدٍ من التدهور، وعرقل وصول المساعدات، وهدد حصول مئات الآلاف من السكان على الغذاء والمياه والرعاية الصحية.ونقلت المنظمة عن هبة مرايف، مديرة مكتبها الإقليمي للشرق الأوسط وشمال أفريقيا، قولها: إن سكان تعز ثالث أكبر مدن اليمن، عانوا سنواتٍ من تداعيات النزاع، فيما تستضيف المدينة أكبر عددٍ من النازحين داخلياً في البلاد. وأضافت أن الحوثيين فرضوا منذ عام 2015 حصاراً على المدينة في فتراتٍ مختلفة، وأغلقوا الطرق الرئيسية التي تربطها بالمدن والبلدات الأخرى، ما اضطر المدنيين إلى استخدام طرقٍ جبليةٍ وعرةٍ وخطرةٍ تفتقر إلى الصيانة. نقص حاد في السلع الأساسية وحذرت مرايف من أن سكان تعز يواجهون مجدداً الحصار ونقصاً حاداً في السلع الأساسية، بما فيها الغذاء والمياه والأدوية، مؤكدةً أن القانون الدولي يلزم الحوثيين بضمان عدم عرقلة وصول المساعدات والمواد الأساسية إلى المدنيين المحتاجين، وتمكين الراغبين في مغادرة المدينة من القيام بذلك بحريةٍ وأمان.وأشارت المنظمة إلى تحذيراتٍ أمميةٍ من نقصٍ حادٍ في الوقود والأكسجين بالمرافق الطبية الحيوية، واحتمال نفاد إمدادات القمح والدقيق خلال أقل من ثلاثة أسابيع، فضلاً عن ارتفاع أسعار المواد الغذائية بنحو 50%، وشح غاز الطهي إلى حدٍ كبير. مرور المساعدات دون عوائق وشددت «العفو الدولية» على أن القانون الدولي الإنساني يلزم جميع أطراف النزاع بالسماح بمرور المساعدات الإنسانية المحايدة إلى المدنيين المحتاجين وتسهيل وصولها بسرعةٍ ودون عوائق، كما يلزمها بالسماح للمدنيين الراغبين في مغادرة المناطق المحاصرة بالخروج منها، وضمان حرية تنقل العاملين في المجال الإنساني المصرح لهم.ودعت المنظمة جميع أطراف النزاع إلى اتخاذ الاحتياطات اللازمة لتجنيب المدنيين والأعيان المدنية آثار العمليات العسكرية، محذرةً من أن تجدد القتال يأتي في وقتٍ يواجه فيه اليمن واحدةً من أسوأ الأزمات الإنسانية في العالم، وسط انهيارٍ اقتصاديٍ وتراجعٍ حادٍ في التمويل الإنساني. تكثيف الضغوط على الحوثيين وفي سياقٍ متصل، دعت مرايف المجتمع الدولي والدول المانحة إلى تكثيف جهود دعم المدنيين في اليمن، وممارسة ضغوطٍ عاجلةٍ ومتكررةٍ على الحوثيين لفتح طرق تعز والإفراج عن جميع المحتجزين تعسفياً لديهم، بمن فيهم العاملون في المجال الإنساني، إلى جانب توفير تمويلٍ عاجلٍ وكافٍ لخطة الاستجابة الإنسانية في اليمن، التي تعاني نقصاً مزمناً في التمويل، تفاقم عقب تقليص المساعدات العالمية عام 2025، وفق المنظمة. وقالت المنظمة إن اتفاق وقف mg.title: Comment la mine de QMM fait grandir l’écosystème économique de la région Anôsy et de Madagascar
mg.description: Quand on pense à une mine, on imagine souvent un site industriel isolé où l’on extrait des ressources du sous-sol. Pourtant, à Fort-Dauphin, l’activité minière de QMM démontre que l’impact d’un tel projet dépasse largement les limites de ses opérations. En structurant une chaîne de valeur globale, l'entreprise est devenue un moteur essentiel du développement de la région Anôsy et de l’économie malgache. Un catalyseur d'emplois et de compétences pour la région L’empreinte économique de QMM commence d’abord par le capital humain. L’activité industrielle agit comme un puissant stabilisateur social et un accélérateur d'emploi sur le territoire. Au-delà des équipes qui opèrent directement sur le site, c’est toute une dynamique de sous-traitance et de services qui prend vie au quotidien. Le tissu entrepreneurial de Fort-Dauphin s'est profondément transformé et professionnalisé. Aujourd'hui, 88 entreprises locales partenaires collaborent avec la mine. Qu'il s'agisse de transport, de logistique, de maintenance industrielle, de sécurité, d'hôtellerie ou de restauration, ces prestataires régionaux représentent à eux seuls environ 1 300 emplois stables. Par un effet de cascade, les revenus injectés circulent dans les commerces de proximité, soutenant l'activité de milliers de familles et créant un écosystème économique interconnecté unique dans le Sud de la Grande Île. Des infrastructures partagées pour le désenclavement et le quotidien L’impact à long terme d’un projet minier se mesure également à l'héritage matériel qu’il laisse au territoire. À Fort-Dauphin, les infrastructures initialement conçues pour la mine ont été pensées pour un usage partagé, devenant de véritables biens publics structurants pour la collectivité. L'exemple le plus emblématique est le Port d’Ehoala. Conçu initialement pour l'exportation des ressources minières, il s'est transformé en un hub maritime régional majeur dont 70 % du trafic est aujourd’hui public, ouvrant la région Anôsy au commerce international. Sur le plan routier, l'engagement de QMM à hauteur de 8 millions USD pour la réhabilitation de la RN13 représente un pas décisif pour le désenclavement et la fluidification des échanges commerciaux. Enfin, la transition énergétique de la ville franchit un cap grâce aux infrastructures associées à la mine, garantissant désormais un accès continu à l’électricité pour près de 80 000 habitants de Fort-Dauphin. Bâtir un avenir durable au-delà de l'exploitation Emplois de qualité, montée en compétences des entrepreneurs locaux, fiscalité citoyenne et infrastructures durables : la valeur créée par QMM dessine les contours d'une croissance inclusive. L’enjeu majeur est désormais de pérenniser les acquis de cet écosystème. En renforçant l'autonomie des entreprises accompagnées et en modernisant les infrastructures de transport et d'énergie, cette dynamique vise à laisser une empreinte économique durable, capable de porter l'essor de la région Anôsy et de Madagascar bien au-delà de la vie de la mine. Mais une mine durable doit veiller à ne pas créer une dépendance à elle seule, c’est ainsi que les projets RSE de l’entreprise visent à renforcer le tissu économique de la région. Levier industriel : injecter de la valeur par le "Contenu Local" Pour faire fonctionner une infrastructure de cette envergure, les besoins en biens et services sont immenses. QMM a fait le choix stratégique de faire du développement de ses fournisseurs nationaux et régionaux un axe majeur de sa contribution économique. En orientant ses dépenses vers le marché malgache, la mine transforme ses coûts d'exploitation en revenus directs pour les entrepreneurs du pays. En 2025, ce sont ainsi 80,88 millions USD qui ont été injectés par QMM dans l’économie nationale à travers ses achats de biens et de services, dont 16,5 millions USD ont été directement fléchés vers les structures locales de la région Anôsy. Cet investissement s'accompagne d'un transfert de compétences rigoureux, permettant aux PME malgaches de se hisser aux standards internationaux de qualité et de sécurité. Parallèlement, QMM participe massivement au budget de l’État et des collectivités décentralisées, avec 11,6 millions USD versés en impôts, taxes, droits et redevances, consolidant ainsi les recettes publiques nécessaires au développement du pays. mg.title: ANTSIRANANA - Le commerce alimentaire soumis aux normes sanitaires
mg.description: Des manquements à l’hygiène ont été relevés dans plusieurs établissements de restauration à Antsiranana. Des sanctions sont prévues en cas de non-respect des règles sanitaires. Une équipe de la direction régionale du commerce et de la consommation, accompagnée des responsables de la sécurité de la Commune urbaine d’Antsiranana, a mené une journée de contrôle dans les boulangeries, les pâtisseries et les gargotes de la ville. Cette opération visait à vérifier les conditions de préparation, de conservation et de vente des aliments, tout en rappelant aux professionnels les règles sanitaires à respecter. Les contrôleurs ont notamment examiné la propreté des lieux et les pratiques de manipulation des denrées. Ils ont rappelé aux vendeurs leurs responsabilités en matière d’hygiène et de protection de la santé des consommateurs. Des gargotes de fortune aux pâtisseries, en passant par les points de vente en bordure de route, les constats sont contrastés. Si certains établissements respectent les règles d’hygiène, d’autres présentent des manquements qui nécessitent des corrections. Des sanctions pourraient être appliquées si ces irrégularités persistent. Selon l’équipe de contrôle, les manquements sont particulièrement fréquents chez les vendeurs installés au bord des routes. Ils concernent aussi bien la propreté des lieux de préparation que l’hygiène des personnes qui manipulent les aliments. Prévention Les responsables ont également sensibilisé les commerçants, les consommateurs et les pêcheurs aux risques d’intoxication alimentaire. À l’approche de l’été austral, ils appellent à une vigilance accrue. Les températures élevées accélèrent la détérioration des aliments périssables lorsque ceux-ci sont mal conservés, ce qui augmente les risques pour les consommateurs. Les contrôleurs ont aussi attiré l’attention sur les intoxications liées aux toxines produites par certaines algues marines. Ces substances peuvent s’accumuler dans les organismes marins, notamment chez les poissons qui se nourrissent d’algues ou d’organismes contaminés. La consommation de produits de la mer contaminés peut provoquer des intoxications graves, parfois mortelles. La directrice régionale du commerce et de la consommation de Diana, Marie-Thérèse Zarasoa, a insisté sur la nécessité de respecter les règles d’hygiène, de rester vigilant dans le choix des denrées et d’appliquer la réglementation pour protéger la Santé publique. La vente de repas à bas prix ou dans des installations sommaires ne dispense aucun professionnel du respect des règles élémentaires d’hygiène. La sécurité sanitaire des aliments reste une obligation pour tous les acteurs du secteur. « Face aux manquements constatés, la sensibilisation devra s’accompagner d’un suivi rigoureux. Les opérateurs qui ne respecteront pas les exigences sanitaires après les rappels nécessaires s’exposeront à des sanctions, conformément à la réglementation en vigueur », a averti la cheffe d’équipe. mg.title: JEAN DE DIEU RANDRIANARIVELO - « Madagascar est un modèle en Afrique »
mg.description: Présent à la huitième édition de l’Alley Hoop de basketball 3x3, à Mahamasina le week-end dernier, l’entraîneur national Jean de Dieu Randrianarivelo dit Coach Deda, répond à nos questions sur la discipline. Jean de Dieu Randrianarivelo, vous êtes venu à l’Alley Hoop pour observer les joueurs. Quel est votre premier constat ? Le talent et la relève sont là à Madagascar. J’ai pu observer plusieurs jeunes joueurs qui méritent un suivi particulier. Certains présentent un gabarit intéressant, avec une taille comprise entre 1,90 m et 2 m. Il faut continuer à repérer ces profils, les accompagner et leur donner les moyens de progresser pour atteindre le haut niveau. Quels sont les principaux aspects à améliorer chez nos joueurs et joueuses ? La priorité est de travailler la condition physique. Le talent seul ne suffit pas pour rivaliser avec les meilleures nations africaines ou mondiales. Nos joueurs doivent être au meilleur de leur forme pour répondre aux exigences du basketball 3x3. Madagascar est un modèle en Afrique et ne peut plus se permettre de perdre du terrain face aux autres pays du continent. Pensez-vous que Madagascar a les moyens de rester compétitif sur la scène continentale ? Oui, nous avons déjà démontré que Madagascar a sa place dans le basketball 3x3 africain. Avec trois sacres chez les hommes, nous sommes le pays le plus titré du continent. Mais nous ne devons pas nous reposer sur nos acquis. Il faut poursuivre le travail, corriger nos points faibles et élever le niveau de nos joueurs, tout en préparant la relève. Pour nous donner les moyens de nos ambitions, nous avons besoin d’une préparation sérieuse et du soutien de l’État. La fédération ne peut pas en assumer seule le coût. Les prochaines échéances continentales sont prévues en décembre. Quelle préparation préconisez-vous ? Madagascar détient le titre chez les dames comme chez les messieurs. Nos adversaires chercheront donc à nous détrôner, à commencer par l’Égypte. À mon avis, la préparation doit commencer dès maintenant, car il faut au moins deux mois pour mettre les joueurs dans de bonnes conditions. Nous pouvons consacrer quatre semaines au travail physique, puis quatre semaines aux aspects technicotactiques. Cette organisation permettrait aux joueurs d’aborder la compétition avec une bonne condition physique et une meilleure maîtrise du jeu. Quel rôle un tournoi comme l’Alley Hoop peut-il jouer dans le développement du basketball 3x3 malgache ? Ce tournoi permet de repérer les talents et d’évaluer le potentiel de nos joueurs. La présence des catégories U18, U23 et seniors offre l’occasion d’observer plusieurs générations. Mais ce travail de détection doit se prolonger par un accompagnement pour aider les joueurs à progresser et préparer la relève du basketball malgache. Donné Raherinjatovo
